XVA SUMMARIZED

Before 2008, pricing a derivative was relatively straightforward:
- Build a pricing model.
- Discount the expected cash flows.
- Execute the trade.

Then the financial crisis happened.

Lehman Brothers collapsed.

Counterparties that were once considered “too big to fail” suddenly defaulted.

Banks realized that a perfectly priced derivative can still lose money if your counterparty fails.

That realization gave birth to XVA.

⸻

DEFINITION

XVA stands for Valuation Adjustments.

Instead of asking, “What is this derivative worth?”

XVA asks, “What is this derivative worth after accounting for every real-world cost and risk?”

Today, almost every major investment bank computes XVA before executing OTC derivative trades.

⸻

FIVE PILLARS OF XVA

1. CVA (Credit Valuation Adjustment)

The expected loss if your counterparty defaults.

Even a profitable trade has value only if the other party survives long enough to pay.

2. DVA (Debt Valuation Adjustment)

The impact of your own institution’s default risk.

Ironically, if your own credit quality deteriorates, certain liabilities become cheaper to settle.

3. FVA (Funding Valuation Adjustment)

Trading isn’t free.

Banks borrow money to fund collateral and hedging activities.

FVA captures those funding costs.

4. MVA (Margin Valuation Adjustment)

Regulations require banks to post initial margin on many derivatives.

That capital cannot be deployed elsewhere.

MVA measures the economic cost of locking up that collateral.

5. KVA (Capital Valuation Adjustment)

Banks must hold regulatory capital against trading exposures.

Shareholders expect a return on that capital.

KVA incorporates the cost of maintaining regulatory capital into the trade price.

⸻

IMPORTANCE OF XVA:

A trade that appears profitable under Black-Scholes can become unprofitable after accounting for:
• Counterparty default
• Funding costs
• Regulatory capital
• Initial margin
• Balance sheet constraints

⸻

WHERE IS XVA USED?

XVA desks exist at nearly every global investment bank.

Applications include:
• OTC Derivatives Pricing
• Interest Rate Swaps
• FX Derivatives
• Credit Derivatives
• Counterparty Risk Management
• Basel III & IV Compliance
• Collateral Optimization
• Capital Allocation

⸻

THE BIGGEST LESSON

Black-Scholes tells you the theoretical value of a derivative.

XVA tells you what it actually costs a bank to trade it.

That’s why XVA has become one of the most concepts in quant finance.
